title: Act I, Scene II

teacherSummary.text: Claudius addresses the court: he has married Gertrude, sends ambassadors to Norway, and lets Laertes return to France but asks Hamlet, still in black, not to go back to university at Wittenberg. Alone, Hamlet wishes he could die and condemns his mother's marriage within two months. Horatio and the guards tell him of the Ghost; he resolves to watch that night.

segments.script: First, meaning. I read “A little more than kin, and less than kind” slowly and put it in my own words: When Claudius calls him "my cousin Hamlet, and my son," Hamlet mutters that they are a little more than kin and less than kind. Next, craft. I notice the wordplay on kin and kind, two words that sound alike but mean family and natural feeling. The strongest word is “kind”: it carries two meanings, "loving" and "natural," and Hamlet denies Claudius both. Then, effect. What does Hamlet's first line reveal about how he feels toward Claudius? My answer: Hamlet's first words are a bitter aside; he resents the hasty marriage that made his uncle his stepfather, and his punning shows the sharp wit he will use as a weapon.

contentNotes.teacherNote: Hamlet wishes his flesh would melt and regrets that God forbids 'self-slaughter.' Use the safe-messaging script; focus on grief and what Hamlet is reacting to. Hamlet calls the marriage 'incestuous sheets' (the period view of marrying a dead husband's brother). This section mentions drinking or a drug (“…at is your affair in Elsinore? We’ll teach you to drink deep ere you depart. My lord, I came to…”). Treat it as period custom or plot detail; name it plainly and don't glamorize it.
